etymology: A place in Egypt, near the shore of the Red Sea, by which Israel encamped before the crossing; the name means “tower,” likely a border-fortress. Also named later by the prophets among the cities of Egypt.
biblical_def: Migdol was a place in Egypt, near the shore of the Red Sea, a landmark of the great crossing. The LORD commanded that Israel “turn and encamp before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, over against Baalzephon” (Exo 14:2). The name means tower, and it was likely a border-fortress on the eastern edge of Egypt. This encampment seemed folly to the eye: hemmed in by the tower on one side, the sea before them, the wilderness on either hand, and Pharaoh’s chariots thundering behind. Israel was trapped, and cried out in terror. But the trap was of God’s own devising, that He might get Himself glory upon Pharaoh and show His people the greatness of His salvation. “Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day” (Exo 14:13). Then the sea was divided, Israel passed through on dry ground, and the waters returned upon the Egyptians. Migdol, the tower by the sea, stands for those extremities into which God leads His people, where every way of escape is shut and nothing remains but to stand still and see Him work. The believer learns at Migdol that God’s corner is His opportunity; when hemmed in on every side, the way forward is not the arm of flesh but the salvation of the LORD, who opens a path through the sea.

etymology: A place in Egypt on the shore of the Red Sea, before which Israel encamped and where they passed through the divided waters; the name is taken to mean “mouth of the gorges” or “place of reeds.”
biblical_def: Pi-hahiroth was a place on the shore of the Red Sea, before which Israel encamped on the eve of the crossing: they were to “encamp before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea” (Exo 14:2). The name is taken to mean the mouth of the gorges, or place of reeds. From this very spot Israel went down into the divided sea: “they departed from before Pihahiroth, and passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness” (Num 33:8). Pi-hahiroth is therefore the threshold of the greatest deliverance of the Old Testament, the type and pattern of redemption itself. Here the people of God, ransomed from the house of bondage, passed through the waters that stood as walls on the right hand and on the left, and came up on the farther shore a free people, while their enemies were drowned behind them. The apostle sees in it a baptism: they were all “baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea”. So Pi-hahiroth preaches the whole gospel of deliverance: that God brings His redeemed safe through the very waters that overwhelm their foes, that the way of salvation lies straight through what seemed sure death, and that the same sea which is a wall of safety to the people of God is a grave to His enemies. The believer, passed through the waters in Christ, sings on the farther shore the song of Moses and the Lamb.

etymology: A wilderness camp of Israel on the border of Moab, one of the stations of the journey; called Iim in its shorter form. The name means “ruins of Abarim” or “heaps of the passes.”
biblical_def: Ije-abarim was a station of Israel’s wilderness journey, on the border of Moab toward the sunrising: “they journeyed from Oboth, and pitched at Ijeabarim, in the wilderness which is before Moab” (Num 21:11), and again in the roll of the stations, “they departed from Oboth, and pitched in Ijeabarim, in the border of Moab” (Num 33:44). The name means ruins, or heaps, of Abarim, the range of hills through which Israel passed toward the plains of Moab. It is one of many camps named in the long itinerary of the wilderness, each a place where Israel pitched the tents, rested a while, and removed again at the moving of the cloud. These station-lists are no idle record; they are the register of a pilgrimage, God leading His people step by step through a great and terrible wilderness toward the promised rest. “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come”. Ije-abarim, a heap of ruins on the edge of Moab, is a fitting emblem of the pilgrim life: the believer pitches no lasting tent in this world, but journeys from station to station, following the pillar of the LORD’s presence, resting where He appoints and moving when He calls, until the wilderness is passed and the land of promise gained. The ruins mark the way; the rest is still ahead.

etymology: The tract of desert at the edge of Egypt into which Israel first journeyed after the Red Sea; named from Etham, the station on its border. Not to be confounded with the encampment of Etham itself.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Etham was the tract of desert on the edge of Egypt into which Israel journeyed just after passing through the Red Sea: “they departed from before Pihahiroth, and passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, and went three days’ journey in the wilderness of Etham, and pitched in Marah” (Num 33:8). It takes its name from Etham, the station on its border, where Israel had camped before the crossing, “in the edge of the wilderness”. Here the redeemed people took their first steps of pilgrimage as a free nation, newly brought out of Egypt with a high hand, following the pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night that the LORD went before them in. It was the beginning of the wilderness school, where God would humble them and prove them, to know what was in their heart, and to teach them that man doth not live by bread alone but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God. The wilderness of Etham thus marks the threshold of the journey between redemption and rest — the long pilgrimage in which God feeds, guides, tests, and disciplines His people. The believer, newly redeemed, likewise enters a wilderness, no longer a slave in Egypt yet not yet come to Canaan, and learns there to walk by the presence of God who leads him all the way.

etymology: The desert before Mount Sinai where Israel encamped and received the law; distinct from the mount itself. It was here the covenant was made and the tabernacle raised.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Sinai was the desert plain before the mountain of God, where Israel encamped for nearly a year and received the law. “In the third month, when the children of Israel were gone forth out of the land of Egypt, the same day came they into the wilderness of Sinai” (Exo 19:1), and there they camped before the mount. It is to be distinguished from Mount Sinai itself, the height on which the LORD descended in fire; the wilderness is the plain at its foot where the people stood. Here the greatest events of the Exodus generation took place: the covenant was made and sealed with blood; the ten commandments were spoken from the fire, the smoke, and the trumpet; the pattern of the tabernacle was given, and the tabernacle raised; the priesthood was ordained. Here too Israel sinned with the golden calf, and here they were numbered and set in order for the march. The wilderness of Sinai is thus the birthplace of Israel as a covenant nation under law. Yet the apostle warns that we are not come to that mount that burned with fire, the mount of terror and of the law that condemns, “but ye are come unto mount Sion…the city of the living God” (Heb 12:22). The believer honors the law given in the wilderness of Sinai, and flees from its curse to the grace of the gospel, from the trembling mount to the Zion of the Mediator.

etymology: A tract of wilderness in the south of Judah, near the town of Maon, where David hid from Saul and was delivered when nearly surrounded; distinct from the town of Maon itself.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Maon was a tract of desert in the south of Judah, near the town of Maon, one of the wild places where David hid during Saul’s long pursuit of him. “They arose, and went to Ziph before Saul: but David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the plain on the south of Jeshimon” (1Sa 23:24). Here David came within a hair’s breadth of capture, for Saul and his men compassed David and his men round about to take them, closing in on either side of a mountain. In that very moment of extremity, God wrought deliverance by an unlooked-for providence: “there came a messenger unto Saul, saying, Haste thee, and come; for the Philistines have invaded the land” (1Sa 23:27), and Saul was forced to break off the chase, so that the place was called the rock of divisions. It was not David’s sword nor his cunning that saved him, but the hand of God moving the Philistines to invade just then. The wilderness of Maon preaches the sure preservation of the LORD’s anointed and of all His people: though the enemy compass them about and the net be all but drawn, God can loose it in a moment by a turn of providence no man foresaw. He suffers His own to be brought to the last strait, then delivers, that they may know their salvation is of Him.

etymology: A tract of wilderness in the south of Judah, near the town of Ziph, where David hid from Saul and where Jonathan came to strengthen his hand in God; distinct from the town of Ziph itself.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Ziph was a desert region in the hill country of Judah, near the town of Ziph, one of David’s hiding-places during Saul’s pursuit. “David abode in the wilderness in strong holds, and remained in a mountain in the wilderness of Ziph” (1Sa 23:14). Twice the men of Ziph betrayed David’s hiding-place to Saul, seeking his favor by giving up the hunted man; yet God suffered them not to prevail. And it was here, in this same wilderness of betrayal and danger, that David was given one of the sweetest comforts of his exile: “Jonathan Saul’s son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God” (1Sa 23:16). Jonathan, though heir to the throne David would inherit, loved him as his own soul, sought him out in his distress, and pointed him to the LORD, assuring him that he should yet be king. So the wilderness of Ziph holds together betrayal and true friendship: the treachery of the Ziphites who sold their neighbor, and the faithfulness of Jonathan who strengthened his friend’s hand in God. It teaches the believer to expect betrayal even from his own countrymen, yet to look for and to be the Jonathan who, in another’s dark hour, comes to point him back to God and strengthen his faith. A word that strengthens a brother’s hand in God is a great mercy in a wilderness.

etymology: A tract of wilderness south of Bethlehem, near the town of Tekoa, where Jehoshaphat’s army went out to meet a great invasion and saw the LORD fight for them; the town was the home of the prophet Amos.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Tekoa was a desert region south of Bethlehem, near the town of Tekoa in Judah. It is remembered for one of the most remarkable deliverances in the history of Judah, in the days of King Jehoshaphat. When a vast alliance of Moab, Ammon, and their allies came up against Judah, Jehoshaphat proclaimed a fast and sought the LORD, and the Spirit assured them the battle was not theirs but God’s. So “they rose early in the morning, and went forth into the wilderness of Tekoa” (2Ch 20:20), and as they went, Jehoshaphat charged them: “Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established; believe his prophets, so shall ye prosper.” Then he set singers before the army to praise the beauty of holiness; and when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushments against the enemy, so that they destroyed one another, and Judah gathered the spoil and returned rejoicing. The wilderness of Tekoa thus preaches the victory of faith and praise: that God’s people prevail not by their own strength but by believing His word and lifting up His praise, while He Himself fights for them. When faith goes out singing, the enemy falls; the battle is the LORD’s, and the shout of praise is the weapon of the trusting.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the victory of faith and praise. Jehoshaphat’s army went into the wilderness of Tekoa believing the LORD and singing His praise; and as they praised, God set ambushments and the enemy fell. The battle is the LORD’s; His people prevail not by strength but by faith, and the shout of praise is the weapon of the trusting.

etymology: A tract of wilderness east of Jordan, near the town of Kedemoth, from which Moses sent messengers of peace to Sihon king of the Amorites; distinct from the town of Kedemoth itself.
biblical_def: The wilderness of Kedemoth was a tract of desert east of Jordan, near the town of Kedemoth, in the days when Israel was drawing near the promised land. From this place Moses sent an embassy of peace to Sihon king of the Amorites: “I sent messengers out of the wilderness of Kedemoth unto Sihon king of Heshbon with words of peace, saying, Let me pass through thy land” (Deu 2:26). Israel asked only leave to pass by on the highway, offering to buy meat and water and to do no harm. But Sihon would not; “the LORD thy God hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into thy hand” (Deu 2:30). Sihon came out to battle, and was utterly destroyed, and his land became the first inheritance of Israel east of Jordan. The wilderness of Kedemoth thus sets before us a solemn mystery: the genuine offer of peace, freely made and wickedly refused, and behind the refusal the sovereign hand of God, who hardened Sihon’s heart in righteous judgment for the fulfilling of His purpose. The offer was sincere; the refusal was Sihon’s own wickedness; and yet God overruled it all, hardening whom He would and delivering the enemy into Israel’s hand. The believer marvels at a sovereignty that leaves the sinner without excuse and yet accomplishes the eternal counsel of God.
webster_summary: A wilderness east of Jordan whence Moses sent peace to Sihon, who refused; a witness to the offer of peace refused and God’s sovereign hardening. Distinct from the town of Kedemoth.

corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness of Kedemoth faces no postmodern redefinition, though it must be distinguished from the town of Kedemoth. The truth its embassy carries answers both the notion that God’s offers are insincere and the notion that the sinner’s refusal is anything but his own wickedness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God’s sovereignty in hardening. Moses sent sincere words of peace to Sihon, who refused of his own obstinacy; yet the LORD hardened his spirit for judgment, delivering him into Israel’s hand. God hath mercy on whom He will, and whom He will He hardeneth — leaving the sinner without excuse, yet accomplishing His eternal counsel.

etymology: A mountain in the far south of Canaan, “that goeth up to Seir,” marking the southern limit of Joshua’s conquest; the name means “the smooth” or “bald mountain.”
biblical_def: Mount Halak was a bare mountain in the far south of Canaan, on the way up to Seir and the land of Edom. It is named as the southern boundary-mark of all the land Joshua conquered: the LORD gave Israel the country “even from the mount Halak, that goeth up to Seir, even unto Baalgad in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon” (Jos 11:17), and again in the summary of the conquered kings (Jos 12:7). The name means the smooth, or bald, mountain. From this bare height in the south to Baal-gad far in the north, the whole breadth of the land was smitten and given into Israel’s hand; Mount Halak marks one end of the measure of God’s faithfulness in fulfilling His promise. “There stood not a man of all their enemies before them; the LORD delivered all their enemies into their hand”. The naming of the two ends of the conquered land, from Halak to Baal-gad, is a witness that God gave what He had sworn, to the full compass of His word, leaving no promise unperformed. The believer reads in Mount Halak the completeness of God’s faithfulness: what He undertakes He finishes, and He that hath begun a good work will perform it, measuring out His mercies from end to end, that His people may possess the whole inheritance He has promised them in Christ.

corruption_summary: A mountain of Scripture marking the bound of the conquest; it recovers the completeness of God’s faithfulness, who performs the whole of His promise.
corruption_paragraphs: Mount Halak faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth its boundary carries answers the doubt that God leaves His promises half-fulfilled, giving a portion and withholding the rest, forgetting that He measures His mercies from end to end.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the completeness of God’s faithfulness. From Mount Halak in the south to Baal-gad in the north, the whole land was given, that Israel might know the LORD performs the full compass of His word. He that hath begun a good work will finish it; God leaves no promise unperformed to His people in Christ.
